questions.question: What is the Python exception hierarchy?
questions.title: Python Exception Hierarchy
questions.direct_answer: All exceptions inherit from `BaseException`; normal application errors inherit from `Exception`, while exit and interrupt signals remain on separate branches.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of inheritance-based matching and the normal application boundary.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating every exception class as unrelated or catching `BaseException` routinely.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choose the narrowest useful branch and explain why exit signals are separate.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `BaseException` is the root of Python's exception tree.
`Exception` is the base for ordinary application and library failures.
A handler for a parent class also catches its descendant classes.
Custom application exceptions normally inherit from `Exception`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python exceptions are classes arranged in an inheritance tree. `BaseException` is the root, but ordinary errors sit under its `Exception` branch. Types such as `ValueError`, `TypeError`, `KeyError`, and `OSError` eventually inherit from `Exception`. This is why `except Exception` catches most failures an application might reasonably report, while it does not normally intercept `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit`, or `GeneratorExit`.

Matching follows inheritance. A handler for `LookupError` catches both `KeyError` and `IndexError`, and a handler for `OSError` catches subclasses such as `FileNotFoundError` and `PermissionError`. For example, a small data importer may handle `FileNotFoundError` specially to report the missing path, then use `except OSError` for other operating-system failures. The more specific clause must come first because Python stops at the first match. The caught object retains its concrete type and useful attributes even when a parent clause handles it.

The hierarchy lets code choose the right level of abstraction. A reusable function should usually catch only the precise failures it can resolve. An outer command-line boundary may catch a broader application-specific base class to produce one consistent error message. User-defined errors should normally inherit from `Exception`, not `BaseException`, so normal application handling includes them without treating them like interpreter exit signals. The hierarchy is therefore both a classification system and the rule Python uses to select handlers.

sections.title: Exception hierarchy and catch boundaries
sections.content:
Every node represents an `isinstance` relationship. A `FileNotFoundError` object is also an `OSError`, an `Exception`, and a `BaseException`. Catching at any of those levels is technically possible, but each wider level throws away some information about what went wrong.

Intermediate parents are useful. `LookupError` groups missing sequence positions and mapping keys. `ArithmeticError` groups numeric failures such as division by zero. `OSError` groups failures reported by the operating system. These families let a boundary apply one policy without listing every leaf, while a lower-level function can still distinguish a specific case.

System-exiting branches sit outside `Exception` so routine error handling does not stop a requested program exit or a user's interrupt. A bare handler crosses that boundary and therefore needs exceptional justification, usually cleanup followed by an immediate re-raise.

sections.title: The branches that matter first
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  B[BaseException] --> E[Exception]
  B --> K[KeyboardInterrupt]
  B --> S[SystemExit]
  B --> G[GeneratorExit]
  E --> V[ValueError]
  E --> T[TypeError]
  E --> L[LookupError]
  L --> KE[KeyError]
  L --> IE[IndexError]
  E --> O[OSError]
  O --> FN[FileNotFoundError]
  O --> PE[PermissionError]
```

sections.title: Observe parent-child matching
sections.content:
```python
errors = [KeyError("id"), IndexError("position"), FileNotFoundError("data.txt")]

assert all(isinstance(error, Exception) for error in errors)
assert isinstance(errors[0], LookupError)
assert isinstance(errors[1], LookupError)
assert isinstance(errors[2], OSError)
assert not issubclass(KeyboardInterrupt, Exception)
```

questions.question: Which built-in Python exceptions should a fresher know?
questions.title: Common Built-in Python Exceptions
questions.direct_answer: The essential built-ins are `TypeError`, `ValueError`, `KeyError`, `IndexError`, `AttributeError`, `ZeroDivisionError`, and common `OSError` subclasses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether common runtime failures can be named and distinguished.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorising names without connecting them to the contract each one represents.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the most specific documented type and keep expected absence separate from defects.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `TypeError` means an operation received an unsuitable type.
`ValueError` means the type is accepted but the value is invalid.
`KeyError` and `IndexError` report missing mapping keys and sequence positions.
`AttributeError` reports a missing attribute; `ZeroDivisionError` reports division by zero.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The most useful built-in exceptions describe the kind of contract that failed. `TypeError` means an operation or function received a type it does not support, while `ValueError` means the type is acceptable but its value is not. `KeyError` reports a missing mapping key, `IndexError` a sequence position outside the valid range, and `AttributeError` an attribute that the object does not provide. Arithmetic includes `ZeroDivisionError`. File operations commonly produce `FileNotFoundError` or `PermissionError`, both under `OSError`.

For example, `int("ten")` raises `ValueError` because strings are valid inputs to `int`, but that string is not a valid integer representation. Accessing `items[10]` in a two-item list raises `IndexError`, while `record["email"]` raises `KeyError` when the key is absent.

These names matter because handling should be specific to a recoverable condition. A missing optional key might have a default, while an invalid required number should be rejected. Catching every built-in under one broad handler loses that distinction. The correct exception is the one that communicates the broken contract to callers and gives them a sensible chance to respond.

sections.title: Exception names are part of an API contract
sections.content:
An exception type tells a caller more than a message string. Code can safely branch on `ValueError` without depending on wording that may change. For that reason, built-in exceptions should be used according to their documented meaning, not simply because they are convenient.

Some operations offer non-exception alternatives. `mapping.get(key)` expresses that a key may be absent, whereas `mapping[key]` expresses that absence is exceptional. Checking `if denominator == 0` can create a domain-specific message before division. Neither style is universally better; the important part is that expected absence and genuine contract failures remain distinguishable.

An unexpected `AttributeError` inside a large handler often signals a programming bug rather than bad user input. Catch only around the operation whose failure you understand, so a real defect keeps its traceback.

sections.title: Match the failure to the exception
sections.content:
| Exception | Broken contract | Small example |
|---|---|---|
| `TypeError` | Unsupported type | `len(10)` |
| `ValueError` | Supported type, invalid value | `int("ten")` |
| `KeyError` | Mapping key absent | `row["id"]` |
| `IndexError` | Sequence position absent | `items[10]` |
| `AttributeError` | Object lacks attribute | `42.append(1)` |
| `FileNotFoundError` | Path does not name a file | `open("missing.txt")` |

sections.title: Handle an expected absence without hiding other errors
